title: Two Delhi Founders Built a Rs 30 Crore Cold Coffee Chain in Two Years
excerpt: Shiv Dhawan and Sohrab Sitaram's First Coffee bet on small-format stores, cold coffee and sub-Rs 300 prices — and grew revenue roughly tenfold in a single year.
body:
• Founded in 2024 by Shiv Dhawan and Sohrab Sitaram, First Coffee has grown to 25 outlets across Delhi, Haryana and Punjab, clocking roughly Rs 30 crore in FY26 revenue — up from about Rs 3 crore in FY25.
  • Cold coffee-based drinks account for 67% of revenue; espresso starts at Rs 195, with cappuccino, latte and flat white priced at Rs 250 — deliberately below big-format specialty cafes.
  • The founders pivoted from a pure grab-and-go model to a hybrid format with 8-10 seats per store, after learning Indian customers still like the option to sit with their coffee.
  • The company has raised $2.5 million across two rounds, including a $1.3 million pre-Series A led by Japan's DG Daiwa Ventures in August 2026, and is targeting Rs 100 crore in revenue in FY27.

Two Delhi entrepreneurs are betting that India's coffee habit does not need a sprawling cafe, a 40-item menu or a Rs 300 bill. Shiv Dhawan and Sohrab Sitaram founded First Coffee in 2024 on a simple thesis: smaller stores, quicker purchases and cold coffee priced below the large specialty chains. The company says it clocked around Rs 30 crore in revenue in FY26 — up from about Rs 3 crore in FY25 — across 25 outlets in Delhi, Haryana and Punjab, according to reporting by Startup Pedia picked up by NDTV Food.

Opening lead: a format reshaped by Indian habits

First Coffee began as a complete grab-and-go concept. The founders soon realised the format needed to fit Indian habits. "We started with pure complete grab-and-go, but then obviously at that time we realised that we were in India and the grab-and-go culture was not mature," Dhawan told Startup Pedia. The brand began adding 8-10 seats at some outlets while keeping stores compact — a hybrid format that keeps convenience at the centre while giving customers the option to sit.

Context & Background: the Keventers playbook, applied to coffee

Sitaram brought more than two decades of hospitality and F&B experience, including a stint at Taj Hotels and a role in scaling Keventers to hundreds of outlets in India and overseas. That background fed into a sharp focus on unit economics and micro-location strategy: before signing a lease, the founders weigh details like whether a store sits on a high street or in a mall, its distance from a PVR, its position near a mall escalator and the food outlets around it.

The first outlet opened at Pacific Outlet Mall in Delhi in April 2024. The chain has since expanded to Gurugram, Faridabad, Chandigarh, Mohali and Rajpura, and now handles around 20,000-25,000 orders every month.

Impact & Analysis: cold coffee does the heavy lifting

While the menu covers espresso, cappuccino, matcha, frappes, smoothies and food, cold coffee-based beverages account for 67% of overall revenue. Seasonal offerings include Vanilla Maple Banana Latte, Mixed Berry Cheesecake Latte, Tiramisu Latte and Orange Americano, alongside Vietnamese coffee, milkshakes, coolers, desserts and breakfast items.

"Rising disposable incomes, greater exposure to global coffee culture and changing consumer preferences have also driven the growth of speciality coffee shops and homegrown coffee brands across the country. However, most coffee brands continue to operate large-format cafes, where customers often pay around Rs 250-300 for a cup."

— Shiv Dhawan, Co-founder, First Coffee

Dhawan's argument: much of that Rs 250-300 price pays for the cafe experience — rent, seating and overheads — rather than the coffee itself. Strip that away and specialty coffee becomes everyday: espresso at First Coffee starts at Rs 195, with cappuccino, latte and flat white at Rs 250.

Investors are buying the thesis. First Coffee has raised $2.5 million across two rounds: a $1.2 million seed round in September 2024 led by BEENEXT; and a $1.3 million pre-Series A round in August 2026 led by Japan-based DG Daiwa Ventures — marking the fund's entry into India's specialty coffee sector — with BEENEXT, Sanjay Kapoor, Shashank Bhagat and angel investors also participating, according to Indian Retailer and The Hindu BusinessLine.

"In the next decade, the size of the out-of-home coffee market in India will grow exponentially, and we want to position ourselves to be right in the middle of this revolution," Dhawan said in the funding announcement.

What's Next

The company is targeting Rs 100 crore in revenue in FY27 — more than a threefold jump — and plans to push beyond major urban centres into Tier 2 cities. Capital from the latest round is earmarked for expansion, hiring, marketing and new products.

With cold coffee driving two-thirds of sales and India's out-of-home coffee market projected to grow at nearly 10% a year through 2032, the founders' small-format wager is about to face its biggest test: whether the model scales as fast as the ambition.
image_caption: The exterior of a First Coffee outlet, the Delhi specialty-coffee brand founded by Shiv Dhawan and Sohrab Sitaram. The company says it reached 25 outlets and roughly Rs 30 crore in FY26 revenue, with cold coffee driving 67% of sales.
nri_angle: No direct diaspora angle — the story is a domestic Indian consumer business — though its small-format, grab-and-go model mirrors the specialty-coffee formats diaspora coffee drinkers know from the US and UK.
author: Diaspora Desk
